title: Molecular Switches & Bacterial Sabotage: Heterotrimeric G-Proteins (Gs/Gi/Gq/G12-13), Adenylyl Cyclase, RGS Accelerators & Cholera/Pertussis Toxins — One-Ångström walks inside Gαt/i–Gβγ (1GOT), Gαs–Adenylyl Cyclase + Forskolin (1AZS), 12-TM AC9–Gαs (6R3Q), and Gαi1–AlF4–RGS4 (1AGR); Rodbell & Gilman's cyc- S49 breakthrough; cholera Arg201 vs. pertussis Cys351; McCune-Albright & GNAS imprinting; and uveal melanoma GNAQ Q209L (darovasertib, FR900359, YM-254890)

teenKit.tldr: A microscopic binary switchboard inside your cells—heterotrimeric G-proteins—controls everything from gut fluid balance to white blood cell traffic, and when hacked by bacteria or mutated by cancer, it triggers massive medical crises.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding these tiny molecular switches reveals how single atomic changes can cause devastating diseases like cholera and metastatic cancer, paving the way for next-generation precision medicines.
keyTakeaways: Heterotrimeric G-proteins act as universal molecular clocks that turn cell signals on and off using GTP binding and hydrolysis.

Bacterial saboteurs like cholera and pertussis target these exact switches chemically, locking them into a permanently active state that floods the body with fluids or traps immune cells in the bloodstream.
Mutations in G-protein genes can cause constitutive locking, leading to rare bone/hormone disorders like McCune-Albright syndrome or aggressive cancers like uveal melanoma.

vocab.meaning: A trio of protein subunits (alpha, beta, gamma) attached to the inside of cell membranes that act as molecular switches for cellular communication.
An enzyme activated by G-proteins that manufactures cyclic AMP, a crucial secondary messenger molecule inside cells.
Regulators of G-protein signaling that act like accelerators to speed up how fast G-proteins shut themselves off.
A mechanical glitch where a protein switch gets stuck permanently in the 'on' position without needing a signal to trigger it.

quiz.question: What is the primary function of heterotrimeric G-proteins in the cell membrane?
options: To physically pump water out of the cell during dehydration
To act as binary molecular switches that transmit outside signals inside the cell
To manufacture DNA code during cellular replication
To directly break down bacterial toxins in the bloodstream
quiz.explanation: G-proteins function as cellular switchboards, relaying external signals into internal biochemical responses.

quiz.question: How do bacterial toxins like cholera and pertussis cause severe disease?
options: By physically eating away at cell walls
By freezing the body's internal temperature
By chemically modifying G-proteins and locking them into a permanently active state
By completely destroying the cell's nucleus
quiz.explanation: These toxins hijack the cell's own machinery by chemically trapping G-protein switches in the 'on' position.

quiz.question: Why does oral rehydration solution (ORS) work so effectively against cholera-induced fluid loss?
options: It neutralizes the cholera toxin directly in the stomach
It uses a cAMP-independent pathway via SGLT1 to pull water and salt back into the body
It closes down the stomach lining completely to stop all digestion
It freezes the adenylyl cyclase enzyme in place
quiz.explanation: ORS bypasses the broken cAMP pathway by hijacking the SGLT1 transporter to absorb water and electrolytes.
